# OneCoin / “Cryptoqueen” Network: Publicly Documented Fraud Scheme and Enforcement Status

## Executive summary

The available sources document OneCoin as an international investment-fraud scheme presented as a cryptocurrency business. According to the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), OneCoin Ltd. began operating in 2014 from Sofia, Bulgaria, and marketed a cryptocurrency called OneCoin through a worldwide multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. Investors were allegedly induced to purchase OneCoin through misrepresentations concerning the cryptocurrency’s value, blockchain, and transaction records. The DOJ states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide between 2014 and 2019 ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

The principal founders identified in the sources are Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood. The DOJ describes both as co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. The second source provides additional detail about Greenwood’s role, describing him as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor and stating that he allegedly received 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, amounting to more than $300 million ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

Greenwood’s enforcement status is comparatively clear in the supplied evidence: he was sentenced to 20 years in prison in 2023 for his role in the OneCoin fraud scheme. The law-firm summary also states that he was ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000, although the DOJ later reported that more than $40 million in forfeited assets was available for victim compensation. Those figures should not be treated as describing the same asset category without further documentation ([Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison); [Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

Ignatova’s status requires greater caution. The DOJ’s 2026 announcement describes her as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and says that the FBI continues efforts to locate her. The 2023 source likewise states that she remained at large at that time. The supplied evidence therefore supports the conclusion that her location and legal status were unresolved in the cited public accounts; it does not establish that she is dead, captured, or definitively living under a particular identity ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

Two sources were supplied:

| Source ID | Source | Date shown in supplied material | Evidentiary character |
|---|---|---:|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of Justice press release concerning OneCoin victim compensation | April 13, 2026 | Primary government source; strongest evidence for the remission process, enforcement agencies, amounts available for compensation, and the government’s stated position on Ignatova |
| S2 | ArentFox Schiff Investigations Blog article concerning Greenwood’s sentence | September 15, 2023 | Secondary legal commentary; useful for Greenwood’s sentence, alleged distributor role, investor count, and specific descriptions of the alleged fraud |

S1 is the more authoritative source for current enforcement and compensation facts because it is an official DOJ announcement. S2 is a law-firm summary rather than a charging document or judgment, and its descriptions of the scheme should be understood as a secondary account of government allegations and sentencing information. The supplied material does not include indictments, trial transcripts, judgments, forfeiture orders, blockchain records, or independent victim affidavits. Conclusions below are therefore limited to what these two sources expressly support.

## Reconstruction of the OneCoin scheme

### Formation, location, and operating period

The DOJ states that OneCoin began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. It was marketed as a cryptocurrency using the same name as the company, OneCoin Ltd. The DOJ identifies the operating period relevant to the remission program as 2014 through 2019 ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

The secondary source similarly states that OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and began operating in the United States around 2015. The word “around” is important: the supplied evidence supports a U.S. presence by approximately 2015, but it does not provide a precise launch date, corporate registration record, or detailed map of the network’s U.S. operations ([Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

### Recruitment and sales model

The scheme allegedly used a global MLM structure. Under the model described by the DOJ, OneCoin members received commissions for recruiting other individuals to purchase cryptocurrency packages. The DOJ characterizes the network as international and states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

S2 provides further detail, stating that OneCoin members were compensated for recruiting new purchasers and that Greenwood was the top MLM distributor. According to that source, Greenwood allegedly earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling more than $300 million. This figure is presented as an allegation or government-described financial benefit in the secondary account, not as an independently verified accounting presented in the supplied material ([Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

The recruitment structure is significant because it linked the sale of purported cryptocurrency to the expansion of the sales network. The sources support describing this as an MLM-based distribution mechanism. They do not, however, provide enough evidence to identify all distributors, determine how compensation was allocated throughout the network, or distinguish every participant’s knowledge and intent.

### Alleged technological and economic misrepresentations

The supplied sources identify two central alleged misrepresentations.

First, S2 states that OneCoin allegedly represented that its value was determined by market supply and demand, while prosecutors said the value was actually set arbitrarily without regard to market forces. This allegation concerns the economic basis of the asset and its purported price discovery ([Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

Second, S2 states that Greenwood claimed OneCoin had a private blockchain capable of identifying OneCoins and recording historical transactions, while prosecutors asserted that no public, verifiable blockchain actually existed. This allegation concerns the technological foundation and auditability of the product being sold ([Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

The DOJ summarizes the conduct more generally as misrepresentations about OneCoin that caused investors to purchase the fraudulent cryptocurrency. The official source does not enumerate every alleged false statement, so the more specific blockchain and valuation assertions should be attributed to the prosecution account summarized by S2 rather than stated as independently established technical findings ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

## Principal founders and roles

### Ruja Ignatova

The DOJ identifies Ruja Ignatova as a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd. and as one of the individuals who, together with Greenwood and others, orchestrated the international investment scheme. The source does not assign her a narrower operational title, such as chief executive, principal marketer, or financial controller. Those roles should therefore not be inferred from the supplied material ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

The DOJ also describes Ignatova as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and says that law enforcement continues to pursue information concerning her location. S2 states that she remained at large as of September 2023. These are enforcement-status facts reported by the sources. They do not prove her present physical location, survival, or guilt beyond the legal proceedings and allegations expressly described in the sources ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

The DOJ identifies Karl Sebastian Greenwood as a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd. S2 adds that he was OneCoin’s top MLM distributor and allegedly earned 5% of monthly sales, totaling more than $300 million. The sources therefore support describing Greenwood as both a founder and a leading participant in the network’s distribution and recruitment model ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

Unlike Ignatova, Greenwood’s enforcement outcome is documented in the supplied evidence. S2 states that he was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in the $4 billion fraud scheme. It also states that he was ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture ([Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

## Scale of the alleged harm

The DOJ states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide. S2 gives a comparable figure—more than $4 billion—and estimates approximately 3.5 million investors. Because the DOJ’s 2026 release does not itself state the 3.5-million figure, that number should be attributed to S2 rather than presented as a figure independently confirmed by both sources ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

The available evidence supports a substantial distinction between the alleged worldwide loss and the assets available for compensation. The DOJ states that more than $40 million in forfeited assets were available for victim compensation. That amount is only a portion of the more-than-$4-billion investment figure reported by the DOJ, although the sources do not provide a final recovery percentage or explain precisely how the available assets were calculated ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

## Enforcement and victim-compensation process

The DOJ states that it filed several OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York and that several key figures had been sentenced. It further states that the government pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the fraud scheme ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

The 2026 announcement concerns remission, a process intended to distribute recovered forfeited assets to eligible victims. According to the DOJ, individuals who purchased OneCoin between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible. The announcement identifies Kroll Settlement Administration LLC as the remission administrator and states that the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the process. The supplied announcement gives June 30 as the petition deadline but does not state the year in the quoted text; the deadline should therefore be reported exactly as supplied rather than assigned a year not expressly provided in the material ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

The DOJ also warns that neither the remission administrator nor the DOJ will ask victims to pay to participate. This warning is particularly relevant because victims of an earlier fraud may be targeted by secondary recovery scams. The source directs prospective claimants to the official remission website and telephone number identified in the announcement ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)).

## Enforcement facts versus unresolved claims

| Issue | Supported enforcement fact | Unresolved or qualified point |
|---|---|---|
| Founders | DOJ identifies Ignatova and Greenwood as co-founders | No more detailed division of Ignatova’s or Greenwood’s founding responsibilities is provided |
| Fraud scale | DOJ reports more than $4 billion invested worldwide | The precise loss calculation and allocation among victims are not supplied |
| Investor count | S2 reports approximately 3.5 million investors | The figure is not stated in S1 and is not independently corroborated in the supplied material |
| MLM operation | Both sources describe a global MLM recruitment and sales structure | The sources do not identify every distributor or establish every participant’s knowledge |
| Technology | S2 reports prosecutors’ allegations concerning the absence of a public, verifiable blockchain | The supplied material does not include technical evidence or an independent audit |
| Greenwood | Sentenced to 20 years in prison; approximately $300,000 forfeiture reported by S2 | The supplied material does not provide the judgment or explain the relationship between that figure and broader forfeited assets |
| Ignatova | Described by DOJ as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive; law enforcement continues seeking her location | The sources do not establish whether she is alive, deceased, captured, or located under another identity |
| Victim recovery | DOJ reports more than $40 million available for compensation | The final amount each claimant will receive and the ultimate recovery rate are not supplied |

## Assessment

On the evidence provided, OneCoin is best characterized as a large-scale, internationally marketed investment-fraud scheme that used the appearance and terminology of cryptocurrency together with an MLM sales structure. The strongest documented facts are the DOJ’s identification of the two founders, the reported scale of victim investment, the existence of multiple Southern District of New York prosecutions, Greenwood’s prison sentence, and the later remission process using forfeited assets ([Source S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [Source S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)).

The evidence does not justify converting every prosecution assertion into an independently verified fact. In particular, the claims concerning the precise absence of a public blockchain, the arbitrary setting of OneCoin’s value, Greenwood’s total alleged earnings, and the exact number of investors should remain attributed claims. Similarly, Ignatova’s status should be described as unresolved in the supplied record: she is reported as wanted and at large, while her actual location and present condition are not established.

## References

ArentFox Schiff. (2023, September 15). *Co-founder of fraudulent cryptocurrency sentenced to 20 years in prison*. ArentFox Schiff Investigations Blog. [https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs. (2026, April 13). *Justice Department announces compensation process for OneCoin fraud victims with funds recovered through asset forfeiture*. [https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)
